newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba fights dengue in one city, no epidemic -govt.
newsitem.headline: Cuba fights dengue in one city, no epidemic -govt.

text.p: Cuban authorities said Wednesday they were fighting an outbreak of dengue fever in this eastern city and about 730 cases of the mosquito- transmitted tropical disease had been detected.
Dr. Francisco Alberto Duran Garcia, director of health for the province of Santiago, told Reuters there had been five or six deaths that may have been related to dengue.
But he said health authorities were still investigating whether these deaths were directly caused by dengue fever or by other causes.
He said the outbreak began two to three weeks ago and was being contained. Three city hospitals were treating the sick and there was sufficient capacity to treat all cases, he said.

In Havana, deputy health minister Ramon Diaz Vallina told reporters 730 to 750 cases had been detected. He added the disease was present only in parts of Santiago, 560 miles (900 km) east of the capital, and nowhere else on the island.
"There is no alarming situation," he said. "It is not an epidemic." Diaz noted dengue was present in some 41 countries.
He said thousands of people had been admitted briefly to hospitals in Santiago, but this was because of a policy of rigorous checking for disease in anyone suffering fever.

The Health Ministry said in a statement that with its long experience of combating such illnesses, Cuba hoped to "eradicate it (the illness) very quickly". It did not mention any deaths from the disease.
The outbreak was Cuba's first since epidemics in 1981 and 1977-78. The 1981 epidemic involved several hundred thousand cases and caused 150 deaths.

Dengue, transmitted by the Aedes Aegypti mosquito, causes headaches and body aches, high fever and a rash and usually lasts for about one week. In its most serious form, which is rare, it can cause haemorrhages and can be fatal.
Duran said there had been about 25 cases of haemorrhagic dengue.

The ministry said numbers of new cases of dengue were falling thanks to efforts to eradicate the carrier mosquito. It said a national campaign was under way to eliminate the mosquito and urged citizens' cooperation.
Measures to counter dengue focus on stopping the spread of the mosquito, using a combination of fumigation and eliminating stagnant pools of water where the insect breeds.
Such efforts have been highly visible in the last few days in Santiago, with teams going from house to house and to public places such as schools fumigating from backpack containers.
A drive to clean streets is under way to prevent water accumulating in discarded containers or behind heaps of garbage.

Residents of the city of more than 400,000 people did not appear alarmed by the outbreak of dengue. Several people interviewed by Reuters said they were grateful for efforts to eradicate the mosquitoes.

Santiago is scheduled to host a Caribbean trade fair next week. Cuban Chamber of Commerce officials said there was no reason to cancel the event and local authorities were preparing stands this week at the central Teatro Heredia where the fair will take place.

Deputy minister Diaz said that while no case of dengue had been reported in Havana, a clean-up programme was under way in the capital, partly to prepare for an international youth festival to be held at the end of July.
